records.place: Atripalda in Irpinia, with Taurasi vineyards at Montemarano, Campania

wine.name: Taurasi Radici Riserva
wine.classification: Riserva of the Taurasi DOCG: four years before release, eighteen months of them in wood
wine.grapes: Aglianico alone, where the Taurasi rules ask for at least eighty five per cent of it.
wine.sites: By the house's recent sheets, a single vineyard at about 550 metres at Montemarano, inside the Taurasi zone, facing south east on calcareous clay; the Riserva is drawn only from the house's Montemarano fruit.
wine.making: Picked by hand in early November. After fermentation the wine spends about thirty months in French barriques and larger Slavonian oak casks, then at least three years in bottle at Atripalda before release, well beyond the four years the Riserva rules ask. A Riserva is made only in the vintages the house judges fine enough.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, dried plum and violet over tar, leather and ash, with tobacco and liquorice as it ages; high acidity and dense, firm tannin carry a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and tannic for its first decade, it opens through its second and can last for decades more; the house's own sheet speaks of sixty years for a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle two hours or more ahead, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Aglianico from the hills around the village of Taurasi in Irpinia, a DOC from 1970 and a DOCG from 1993.
Aged at least four years before release, eighteen months of them in wood, by the DOCG's rules.
Italian for roots: the name the house has given its Taurasi since the 1986 vintage.

records.table: Mastroberardino's Taurasi Radici Riserva is Aglianico alone from a high vineyard at Montemarano, aged about thirty months in oak and three years in bottle before it leaves Atripalda. Sour cherry, tar and firm tannin: decant it, and give it a decade.
records.story: The family has made wine at Atripalda, by its own account, since the middle of the eighteenth century, and in 1878 a forebear registered the firm with the Avellino Chamber of Commerce and began to send its wines abroad. Through the twentieth century, while Irpinia's old grapes came close to disappearing, the house held to Aglianico, Fiano and Greco, and two brothers of the family ran it together through the decades after the Second World War. Taurasi, the Aglianico of the hills around the village of Taurasi, became a DOC in 1970 and a DOCG in 1993. From the 1986 vintage, by most accounts, the house gave its Taurasi the name Radici, roots, keeping a Riserva for the years it judged fine enough. In 1994 the brothers parted: one kept the name and the Atripalda cellar, the other took much of the family's vineyard land and founded Terredora. Two years later the house began, with the archaeological authorities, to replant vines inside the excavations of Pompeii, and the first Villa dei Misteri followed with the 2001 vintage. Radici Riserva is Taurasi as the house has long made it: slow, firm and held for years before release, the bottle to open when a guest asks what Aglianico becomes with time.

others.name: Taurasi Radici
others.note: The house's Taurasi without the Riserva's longer keeping, from its vineyards at Montemarano and Mirabella Eclano.

others.name: Fiano di Avellino Radici
others.note: The house's Fiano under the same name, the white it held to when the grape was close to lost.

others.name: Villa dei Misteri
others.note: Piedirosso with Sciascinoso from vines replanted inside Pompeii, first made with the 2001 vintage.

traps: Taurasi is Aglianico from Campania; Aglianico del Vulture is the same grape across the border in Basilicata.
Terredora is not a second label of Mastroberardino: it was founded by the brother who left the family firm in 1994.
The house gives the name Radici to a Fiano as well, so say Taurasi Radici Riserva in full.

cards.front: Mastroberardino's Taurasi Radici Riserva: how long in wood and in bottle before release?
cards.back: About thirty months in French barriques and Slavonian casks, then at least three years in bottle.

cards.front: What did Mastroberardino begin inside the excavations of Pompeii in 1996?
cards.back: The replanting of vines with the archaeological authorities; the first Villa dei Misteri followed with the 2001 vintage.

questions.q: A guest asks where the grapes for Mastroberardino's Taurasi Radici Riserva grow. What do you tell them?
opts: A high vineyard at Montemarano in Irpinia
The lower slopes of Vesuvius above Naples
Terraces above the sea at Furore
The Vulture volcano in Basilicata
questions.exp: The house's sheets give a single vineyard at about 550 metres at Montemarano, inside the Taurasi zone; Vulture is Aglianico's other home, in Basilicata, and its wine can never be Taurasi.

questions.q: In 1994 the family firm of Mastroberardino split in two. What did the brother who left go on to do?
opts: Found Terredora with much of the vineyard land
Take over the estate of Feudi di San Gregorio
Replant the vineyards inside Pompeii
Sell his share to an Avellino cooperative
questions.exp: One brother kept the name and the Atripalda cellar while the other took much of the vineyard land and founded Terredora; the Pompeii vineyards were Mastroberardino's own project, begun in 1996.

report: The house's family page gives the eighteenth century roots at Atripalda and the registration of 1878 with the Avellino Chamber of Commerce; Wikipedia dates the house to 1878 as well, so founded is 1878 where the library leaves it empty.

The Taurasi DOC of 1970, the DOCG of 1993 and the Riserva's four years with eighteen months in wood rest on the disciplinare (Regione Campania and the AIS copy); one trade account gives 1992 for the DOCG.
Radici from the 1986 vintage rests on Rare Wine Co and the Decanter note quoted on Wine.com's Radici Riserva page; a merchant lists a Taurasi Radici 1985, so the story says by most accounts.

The Riserva's single vineyard at Montemarano is from the house's 2026 sheet; the standard Radici draws on Montemarano and Mirabella Eclano by the house's grappa page and an importer, and Rare Wine Co says the Riserva takes only the Montemarano lots. The bottle time is 36 months on older sheets and about 42 on the newest, so the record says at least three years.

The brothers who ran the house are described, not named: one died in January 2014 aged eighty six by two trade accounts, but no source read gave his birth year, and the accounts that did are a writer's own site; the other's death was reported by Fanpage without a date read here. The founder of 1878 has no dates in any source read and is described as a forebear.
The Pompeii project of 1996 and the first Villa dei Misteri of 2001 rest on Decanter and Jancis Robinson's site; the house's head who led it is living and is not named.
The region record's producers line says the house's Taurasi vintages of the 1960s proved the wine could age; no source read here gave that, so the record does not say it.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, all on the house's domain or the open web; no fetch tried.

records.place: Sorbo Serpico, Irpinia, Fiano di Avellino DOCG, Campania

wine.name: Fiano di Avellino Pietracalda
wine.classification: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, granted to Fiano di Avellino in 2003
wine.grapes: Fiano, from the one Pietracalda vineyard.
wine.sites: The Pietracalda vineyard in the house's home commune of Sorbo Serpico, between about 400 and 600 metres on clay and limestone soils, by the house's own sheet; Pietracalda is Italian for hot stone.
wine.making: The juice is fermented in stainless steel at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius and the wine never sees wood. The house's earlier sheets give four to five months in steel on the fine lees with repeated stirring; its sheet for the 2022 vintage, labelled Riserva, gives twelve months on the lees in steel and three in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Pear, quince and hazelnut over acacia blossom and a smoky, struck flint edge, with a waxy texture, fresh acidity and a long, saline finish; honey and toasted nuts come with age.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open within a year or two of the harvest, it gains honey, beeswax and toasted hazelnut over five to ten years in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, as the house's own sheet suggests; no need to decant; a white wine glass with room for its perfume.

label.means: Fiano from the hills around Avellino in Irpinia: a DOC from 1978 and a DOCG from 2003.
Printed on the 2022 vintage by the house's sheet: at least a year of ageing before release, by the DOCG's rules.
The single vineyard at Sorbo Serpico whose name the wine carries.

records.table: Feudi di San Gregorio's Pietracalda is Fiano di Avellino from one high vineyard at Sorbo Serpico, fermented and kept on its lees in steel with no oak. Pear, hazelnut and a smoky edge over fresh acidity: pour it cool, and expect it to gain honey with age.
records.story: Fiano di Avellino, the white of the hills around the city, became a DOC in 1978. Eight years later, in 1986, two families of the province founded Feudi di San Gregorio at Sorbo Serpico, as the house tells it, and made the province's grapes in a modern cellar: clean fruit, cool fermentation in steel and, for the whites, a long rest on the lees. Beside its Fiano and Greco the house made an Aglianico from old vines, Serpico, and a Merlot, Pàtrimo. Pietracalda is the Fiano of a single vineyard in the house's home commune, high on clay and limestone and never touched by oak: fermented cool in steel and left on its fine lees for texture. In 2003 Fiano di Avellino became a DOCG. In 2004 the house opened a new winery at Sorbo Serpico, the work of a Japanese architect. Later vintages of Pietracalda were labelled Riserva and kept a full year on their lees, by the house's own sheet for the 2022. Pietracalda is the white to pour when a guest asks what Fiano is: grown high in Irpinia, made without wood, and able to age.

others.name: Serpico
others.note: Aglianico from old vines, labelled Irpinia Aglianico rather than Taurasi; the house's red statement.

others.name: Greco di Tufo Cutizzi
others.note: The house's Greco from the Tufo hills, firmer and more citrus peel than its Fiano.

others.name: Taurasi Piano di Montevergine Riserva
others.note: The house's Taurasi, from its estate inside the DOCG.

traps: Fiano is waxy and nutty, Greco firmer and more citrus peel: do not swap Pietracalda for Cutizzi.
Serpico is Aglianico grown in Irpinia but is not Taurasi; Pietracalda is the house's Fiano, never its red.
Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo are separate DOCGs, not two styles of one wine.

cards.front: Feudi di San Gregorio's Pietracalda: what vessel, and how long on the lees?
cards.back: Stainless steel and no oak; four to five months on the lees in earlier sheets, a year for the Riserva of 2022.

cards.front: In what year, and in which Irpinian commune, did two families found Feudi di San Gregorio?
cards.back: In 1986, at Sorbo Serpico in the province of Avellino.

questions.q: A guest who dislikes oaky whites asks about Feudi di San Gregorio's Pietracalda. What do you tell them?
opts: It is fermented in steel and kept on its lees
It is fermented and aged in new barriques
It spends a year in large chestnut casks
It is aged under flor like a Fino
questions.exp: The house's sheets give fermentation and ageing in stainless steel on the fine lees, with no wood; its texture comes from the lees, not from new barriques.

questions.q: Feudi di San Gregorio was founded in 1986, eight years after Fiano di Avellino became a DOC. When did Fiano di Avellino become a DOCG?
questions.exp: The DOCG was approved by decree in July 2003; 1993 is the year Taurasi became a DOCG, and 1970 the year of its DOC.

Feudi di San Gregorio: Discover our winery
Feudi di San Gregorio: Pietracalda technical sheet
Feudi di San Gregorio: Pietracalda Fiano di Avellino DOCG Riserva 2022 sheet
Regione Campania: Fiano di Avellino DOCG production rules

report: The plan's note asked to confirm Pietracalda against Serpico: Serpico is the house's red statement and, with Pàtrimo, is named among its wines of the late 1990s by Vinography and Escapement Magazine; Pietracalda is kept because the group otherwise has no Fiano di Avellino, the library calls it a widely poured Fiano, and Taurasi is already Mastroberardino's. No swap proposed, but the integrator may weigh Serpico.

The founding of 1986 by two Irpinian families and the new winery of 2004 rest on the house's own pages; the Japanese architect, the founding families and the owners are living or not dated and are not named.
The DOC of 27 April 1978 and the DOCG of 18 July 2003 rest on the disciplinare (Regione Campania and the AIS copy); the Riserva's year of ageing on two secondary summaries of it.

The vineyard's height and soils, the steel, the lees and the service temperature are the house's sheets; the earlier English sheet gives four to five months on the lees, the 2022 Riserva sheet twelve, so both are told. The vineyard's size (8 or 10 hectares) and the vines' age are left out as volatile; the volcanic soil one retailer gives is left out against the house's clay and limestone.

Left out for want of a source: the first vintage of Pietracalda (the house's first wines are dated 1991 and its first Fiano 1992 by one account only), the grape share beyond Fiano, the label designer and the earthquake of 1980 as the founders' spur.
The library's why calls the house the modern face of Campania and its Fiano a benchmark: a judgement word, reported for the integrator and not edited.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, two of them restricted to the house's own domains.

records.place: San Cipriano Picentino, in the hills above Salerno, Campania

wine.name: Montevetrano
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the category below DOC and DOCG
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the larger part, with Merlot and about a tenth of Aglianico; the first vintages were Cabernet with a little Aglianico alone.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards on the hills of San Cipriano Picentino, facing south west, below a medieval castle.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel after about a seventh of the juice is drawn off, with frequent punching down and some twenty days on the skins; the malolactic follows. The wine then ages for eight to fourteen months by vintage in 225 litre French oak barriques, most of them new, and six months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Cassis, black cherry and graphite over tobacco leaf and dark chocolate, with the ashy, sour cherry edge of Aglianico; full and polished, with ripe, firm tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Approachable after five years or so, it goes on developing for fifteen to twenty years in bottle, as the estate itself suggests.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The Indicazione Geografica Tipica named for the hills of Salerno, under which the estate sells its Cabernet led blend.
The name of the estate and of its flagship red alike.

records.table: Montevetrano is a small estate's blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Aglianico from the hills above Salerno, first made in 1991 and first sold from 1993. Dark and polished, with an ashy Aglianico edge, it wants decanting and a Bordeaux glass.
records.story: Montevetrano grew from a friendship. In the middle of the 1980s, as the estate tells it, a group of wine lovers set out to experiment at a family property at San Cipriano Picentino, in the hills above Salerno, below a medieval castle. With the advice of a consultant oenologist they planted Cabernet Sauvignon beside Aglianico, in a region whose classic red was Aglianico. After six years of work in the vineyard, the first bottles, of the 1991 vintage, were Cabernet with a little Aglianico and were made only for friends; a few more followed from 1992, and 1993 is the vintage the estate gives as its first for sale. By the middle of the 1990s Merlot had joined the blend, which settled at about six parts Cabernet to three of Merlot and one of Aglianico, all from the estate's own vines and aged in new French barriques. The wine is sold as Colli di Salerno IGT, outside the rules of any DOC: a Bordeaux blend with a Campanian accent. For a sommelier it is the southern answer to the Super Tuscans: international grapes, a shadow of Aglianico, and the estate's own name on the label.

others.name: Core
others.note: The estate's red from Aglianico alone, the grape that seasons the flagship.

traps: Montevetrano is an IGT, Colli di Salerno, not a Campanian DOCG such as Taurasi.
Its Aglianico is a seasoning, about a tenth of the blend, not the base.
The 1991 was made only for friends, and 1993 is the first vintage given for sale, so both years appear in accounts of the first Montevetrano.

cards.front: Montevetrano: which three grapes, and which leads the blend?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with Merlot and about a tenth of Aglianico.

cards.front: What became of Montevetrano's 1991, its opening vintage?
cards.back: It was bottled only for friends; 1993 is the vintage the estate gives as its first for sale.

questions.q: A guest who knows Taurasi asks how the blend of Montevetrano is built. Which answer is right?
opts: Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot and Aglianico
Aglianico, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot
Merlot, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Aglianico
Piedirosso, with Aglianico and Merlot
questions.exp: Cabernet Sauvignon is the larger part, with Merlot and about a tenth of Aglianico; Merlot joined only in the 1990s, and Aglianico is the seasoning, not the base.

questions.q: Montevetrano's first vintage was bottled in tiny quantity, only for friends. Which year was it?
questions.exp: The 1991 came after six years of work in the vineyard and went only to friends; 1993 is the vintage the estate gives as its first for sale.

report: The library's holdings for p-montevetrano name the founder, who is living and is in people.json; the record describes the group of friends instead, and the library line is reported for the integrator, not edited.

The first vintage is 1991 on the estate's 1996 and 1998 pages and 1993 on its 2000 and 2010 pages and its 2018 sheet; Superiore.de and Scatti di Gusto say the 1991 and 1992 went only to friends and 1993 was the first sold, so the record tells both.

The first blend is ninety parts Cabernet to ten of Aglianico on the estate's home page and in two trade accounts, seventy to thirty in one; the record says Cabernet with a little Aglianico. Merlot is in the 1996 sheet's blend of sixty, thirty and ten; its first year is not known.

The medieval castle above the estate rests on two retailer accounts (Superiore.de and Bottle of Italy); one says the wine is named for it, a single source, so the record does not say so. The estate's history page dates its start to 1983 by one summary, so founded is left empty.

The making is the estate's sheets: steel after a drawing off of about fifteen per cent, some twenty days of fermentation and maceration, eight to fourteen months in 225 litre barriques by vintage, new in most and new and second use in 2011, and six months in bottle.

DoctorWine reports a sale of the estate to Tenuta Ulisse; the date was not read and a present owner is volatile, so it is left out for the integrator. The region record's producers line says the wine showed the south could make a world class wine: a judgement word, reported, not edited.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35, two of them restricted to the estate's own domain.

wine.name: Furore Bianco Fiorduva
wine.classification: Costa d'Amalfi DOC since 1995, with Furore one of its three named subzones
wine.grapes: Ripoli, the larger part, with Fenile and Ginestra in about equal shares: three old grapes of the Amalfi coast.
wine.sites: Terraces cut into the cliffs of Furore and its neighbouring communes, from about 200 to 550 metres, facing south over the sea on dolomitic limestone rock, worked by hand.
wine.making: The grapes are picked by hand late, in the last ten days of October, and pressed gently, and the juice is settled cold. It then ferments slowly at about 12 degrees Celsius in oak barriques, for about three months by one of the house's sheets; another gives six months in small oak casks before bottling.
wine.glass: Candied apricot, citrus peel and dried wild herbs over honey and a salty, sea spray edge; full and rounded, with fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous from its release, it keeps and gains depth for several years in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with a generous bowl.

label.means: The DOC of the Amalfi coast, approved in 1995, with Furore, Ravello and Tramonti as named subzones.
The subzone named for the cliff village where the house stands and the grapes grow.
White; Fiorduva is the house's late picked selection, apart from its plain Furore Bianco.

records.table: Fiorduva is Marisa Cuomo's white from the cliff terraces of Furore on the Amalfi coast: Ripoli, Fenile and Ginestra, picked late and fermented in oak barriques. Apricot, wild herbs and sea salt give it the weight for richer fish; pour it cool, not cold.
records.story: Furore is a village strung down the cliffs of the Amalfi coast, where vines grow on narrow terraces above the sea. By the house's account, a Furore family founded the estate in 1942, and in 1980 a man of the family gave it to his bride as a wedding gift and put her name on it; one account dates the gift to 1983, after he bought out his relatives' shares in 1980. The cellar was dug into the dolomitic limestone of the cliff. The house worked the coast's own grapes: Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli for its whites, Piedirosso and Aglianico for its reds, grown on terraces worked entirely by hand. In 1995 the Costa d'Amalfi became a DOC, with Furore, Ravello and Tramonti as its named subzones, and the house's wines carry the Furore name. Fiorduva is its white of the Furore subzone: the three grapes picked late in October and fermented slowly in oak. It matters because of where it comes from: a few terraces between the mountains and the sea, and grapes found almost nowhere else, which survive because the ground was too steep to replant.

others.name: Furore Rosso
others.note: Piedirosso with Aglianico from the same terraces, the red side of the house.

others.name: Furore Bianco
others.note: The house's plain white of Furore, made apart from Fiorduva.

traps: Fenile, Ginestra and Ripoli are grape names, not vineyard names.
Costa d'Amalfi is one DOC with three named subzones, Furore, Ravello and Tramonti; Furore is not a DOC of its own.
Marisa Cuomo is the house's name on the label; the wine itself is Fiorduva, and the plain Furore Bianco is another bottle.

cards.front: Marisa Cuomo's Fiorduva: which three grapes go into it?
cards.back: Ripoli, the larger part, with Fenile and Ginestra: three old grapes of the Amalfi coast.

cards.front: Into what rock was the cellar of the Furore house that makes Fiorduva dug?
cards.back: The dolomitic limestone of the Furore cliffs.

questions.q: A guest asks how Fiorduva gets its weight and its rounded texture. Which answer fits the making?
opts: Late picking and a slow fermentation in barriques
Long skin contact in clay amphorae
Ageing under flor in a solera
A second fermentation in the bottle
questions.exp: The grapes are picked late in October and fermented slowly at low temperature in oak barriques, by the house's sheets; there is no skin contact in amphora and no flor.

questions.q: By the account of the house that makes Fiorduva, what happened to the Furore estate in 1980?
opts: It was given to a bride as a wedding gift
It was bought by a Naples cooperative
A landslide destroyed its old cellar
The Costa d'Amalfi DOC was approved
questions.exp: The house says the estate was given in 1980 as a wedding gift and named for the bride; the Costa d'Amalfi DOC came only in 1995.

sources.title: Marisa Cuomo: Azienda
Marisa Cuomo: Furore Bianco Fiorduva
Marisa Cuomo: The Company
AIS: Costa d'Amalfi DOC production rules
Wine Spectator: Air-oir on the Amalfi Coast

report: The house is named for a living woman, so the record keeps her name only as the house's name and describes the couple; her husband is living too and is not named, nor is the house's consultant oenologist.

The house's Azienda page gives the family's wine from 1942 and the wedding gift of 1980; its home page gives 1980 as the founding year, the library's; Wine Spectator has the relatives bought out in 1980 and the gift three years later, so the story gives both.

The blend, the terraces of 200 to 550 metres facing south on dolomitic limestone, the harvest in the last ten days of October, the cold settling and the slow fermentation at 12 degrees Celsius in barriques are the house's own pages; one sheet gives about three months in barrique, another six months in small casks, so both are told. An International Wine Challenge entry calls the 2018 unoaked, against the house; the record follows the house.
The cellar dug into dolomitic limestone rests on the house's company page and a visitor's account whose address names a living man, so it is not cited.

The DOC of 10 August 1995 and its subzones Ravello, Tramonti and Furore rest on the disciplinare (AIS copy); the communes of the Furore subzone are given by one secondary guide only, so the record does not list them.

Left out for want of a source: the first vintage of Fiorduva (1995 was not found anywhere), the meaning of its name, pergola training and ungrafted vines. The fetch of the house's site was refused by the network and not retried.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, two of them restricted to the house's own domain.

records.place: Cellole, Falerno del Massico DOC, on the slopes of Roccamonfina, Campania

wine.name: Falerno del Massico Vigna Camarato
wine.classification: DOC since 1989, for five communes of Caserta province
wine.grapes: Aglianico, about four fifths, with Piedirosso for the rest, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: The single Camarato vineyard at San Castrese, on the slopes of the extinct Roccamonfina volcano, planted in 1965 by the house's account.
wine.making: Picked in the last ten days of October and made only in the years the house judges strong enough. After fermentation the wine ages for twelve to eighteen months in Allier oak barriques, about a third of them new and the rest in their second or third year, then as long again in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and violet over tobacco, liquorice and a smoky, savoury edge; full bodied, with Aglianico's high acidity and firm tannin and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed in its first years, it lasts fifteen to twenty years in a strong vintage, by the house's own sheet.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The DOC of 1989 named for the Roman Falernian, from five communes of Caserta province.
Vigna means vineyard: the wine of the one Camarato vineyard at San Castrese.
Red; the DOC also allows a white and a Primitivo.

records.table: Vigna Camarato is Villa Matilde's single vineyard Falerno del Massico: Aglianico with some Piedirosso from the slopes of the Roccamonfina volcano, made only in strong years and aged in barriques. Dark, firm and savoury, it wants decanting and years in the cellar.
records.story: The Romans prized Falernian, grown on the slopes of Monte Massico, the Mons Falernus of old; Pliny, Horace and Martial wrote of it, and its Opimian vintage of 121 BC was poured decades after the harvest. The wine then vanished for centuries, and accounts differ on which grapes made it. In the 1960s, as the house tells it, a lawyer with a passion for old wines and for the Latin authors set out to bring Falernian back. With friends, professors of the University of Naples among them, he searched the district for vines that had survived phylloxera at the end of the nineteenth century, and the stock he found was replanted on the Massico. The estate he built took the name Villa Matilde. Its Falerno del Massico, first made with the 1975 vintage by the house's sheet, came before the law: the DOC followed in 1989. The Camarato vineyard at San Castrese, planted in 1965, gave a wine of its own from the 1981 vintage, made only in strong years. In 1985 the founder's children took charge. Vigna Camarato is the bottle to open when a guest asks about Falernian: a modern wine of Aglianico and Piedirosso from the same hills, not a copy of a Roman one.

others.name: Falerno del Massico Rosso
others.note: The estate's younger red of Aglianico and Piedirosso, first made with the 1975 vintage, partly aged in large Slavonian casks.

others.name: Falerno del Massico Bianco
others.note: Falanghina from the same hills, the white of the revival.

traps: Falerno del Massico is a DOC of 1989; the Roman Falernian is only its namesake, and accounts differ on which grapes made it.
Vigna Camarato is Aglianico led; Villa Matilde's Falerno del Massico Bianco is Falanghina, so the name Falerno does not tell a colour.
Roccamonfina, the extinct volcano of the Falerno vineyards, is not Vesuvius, the volcano above Naples.

cards.front: Villa Matilde's Vigna Camarato: which grapes, and on what volcano's slopes?
cards.back: Aglianico, about four fifths, with Piedirosso, from the Camarato vineyard on the slopes of Roccamonfina.

cards.front: Which wine of ancient Rome did the founder of Villa Matilde set out in the 1960s to bring back?
cards.back: Falernian, the wine of Monte Massico that Pliny and Horace wrote of.

questions.q: A guest asks what sets Villa Matilde's Vigna Camarato apart from the estate's plain Falerno Rosso. Which answer is right?
opts: One vineyard, strong years only, and barriques
Falanghina in place of Piedirosso in the blend
A long ageing under flor in the cellar
Grapes bought from growers across Caserta
questions.exp: Vigna Camarato comes from the single Camarato vineyard, made only in strong years and aged twelve to eighteen months in barriques; the plain Rosso is partly aged in large casks, and neither holds Falanghina.

questions.q: Villa Matilde's founder searched the Massico in the 1960s with friends from the University of Naples. What were they looking for?
opts: Vines that had survived phylloxera
Cabernet planted by Napoleon's officers
Grapes for a sparkling wine of Naples
Vines brought from Tuscany after the war
questions.exp: As the house tells it, they sought stock that had outlived phylloxera at the end of the nineteenth century, to replant the vines of the Roman Falernian on the Massico.

report: The house is not in the library. Its revival of the 1960s, the friends from the University of Naples, the vines that survived phylloxera, the second generation in 1985 and the white of Falanghina are the house's history page; the lawyer and the 1960s are also in A Dozen Ultimate Vineyards' Behind the label and Regal Wine Co.

The founder is described, not named: his death is given as 2006 by one account only and no birth year was found, and his name is also borne by a living grandson in the business; his children who took charge in 1985 are living. The estate's naming for his wife rests on one account and is left out; founded is left empty, 1963 being in one listing only.

Vigna Camarato's blend of four fifths Aglianico and one of Piedirosso, the San Castrese vineyard planted in 1965, the first vintage of 1981, strong years only, the late October harvest, twelve to eighteen months in Allier barriques a third new and as long in bottle, and fifteen to twenty years of life are the house's own sheet. One review calls an estate red Aglianico alone; the record follows the house.
The DOC of 3 January 1989 and its five communes rest on the disciplinare (AIS copy); its grape rules for the Rosso were not read, so the record does not state them.

Falernian on Monte Massico, the Mons Falernus, the writers who praised it and the Opimian vintage of 121 BC rest on Wikipedia and the Wein.plus glossary; the grapes of the Roman wine are disputed, so the record says so.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35, two of them restricted to the house's own domain.
